opus-5.5.text:
I think we're going to see a really wide range, honestly. One of the things I'm most excited about is that if you can develop a general-purpose robotic foundation model, one that learns from data across many different platforms, then you lower the barrier to building new kinds of hardware. Right now, if you design a new robot, you basically have to start from scratch on the software and intelligence side, and that's a huge tax. If the intelligence can transfer, then people can design robots that are really well suited to a particular job without paying that cost every time.

So I imagine you'll have some fairly simple, low-cost arms that do a lot of useful things, maybe mounted on a table or a mobile base. You'll have mobile manipulators in homes and warehouses. You'll probably have humanoids in some settings, because the world is built for human bodies and there's something appealing about that. But I don't think humanoids are going to be the only answer, or even necessarily the dominant one. In a lot of cases, two arms, some wheels, and a decent camera setup get you a lot of the way there, and it's cheaper and more reliable.

I also think we'll see form factors we haven't really imagined yet. When intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, hardware designers get much more creative freedom: robots specialized for agriculture, for surgery, for cleaning, or things with unusual numbers of arms or different kinds of grippers. In our own work we've seen that models trained on data from many robot embodiments can actually do better than models trained on just one, which suggests a single brain can drive a lot of different bodies. That's what makes me optimistic that the ecosystem will get much more diverse over time, not converge on one design.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that transferable intelligence across robot platforms will lower the cost of new hardware and lead to a much wider, more diverse range of robot forms.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots specialized for cleaning and other fields, but does not envision household robots specialized for particular tasks in a way analogous to kitchen appliances.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most interesting questions in the field right now, and honestly I think a lot of people have the causality backwards. There's this assumption that you pick the form factor first and then you build the intelligence for it. And I actually think it's going to go the other way, that as the intelligence gets more general, the form factor becomes much more of a free variable.

If you look at the history of robotics, the hardware was almost always designed around the limitations of the software. You'd build a very specific gripper for a very specific task because the controller could only really do that one thing. And so the diversity of robots we have in the world today is kind of a reflection of how narrow the intelligence has been.

What's changed is that we're starting to see models that can transfer across embodiments. At Physical Intelligence, and in the academic work before that, one of the things that surprised me the most was how much a policy trained on one robot could help a totally different robot, with a different number of arms, a different gripper, a different camera setup. And once you have that property, you're no longer locked in. You can let the application drive the design.

So where does that lead? I think humanoids will exist, and there's a real argument for them, which is that the world was built for human bodies. Doorknobs, stairs, kitchen counters, all of it. But I'm a little skeptical of the view that humanoids are the end state for everything. Legs are expensive and failure-prone, and a lot of the work we actually want done, like in a kitchen or a warehouse or a lab, doesn't require walking. It requires good hands and good perception, and the base can be a wheeled platform that costs a tenth as much.

So my guess is you end up with a spectrum. On one end, fairly general-purpose mobile manipulators, maybe some humanoid, many not, that can handle a long tail of tasks in homes and businesses. In the middle, a lot of purpose-built but still intelligent machines, where the form factor is optimized for a domain but the brain is shared with everything else. And then at the far end, things that look nothing like what we picture when we say "robot." Soft robots, very small robots, things embedded in furniture or vehicles or buildings.

The thing I'd emphasize is that the hardware will probably diverge, but the data and the models will converge. We'll see a lot of different bodies, but increasingly they'll be running variants of the same underlying intelligence, and every new body will make that intelligence a little bit better for all the others. That flywheel is what I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that more general intelligence will free form factor choices and lead to many different robot bodies sharing related models.

r002.rationale: It mentions purpose-built machines optimized for a domain and robots working in kitchens, but does not envision separate robots specialized for particular household tasks like kitchen appliances.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see a pretty wide range of form factors. Humanoids are compelling because we’ve built our environments around humans. If you want a robot to use the same tools, reach the same shelves, and move through the same spaces that we do, having a human-like body makes sense. But that doesn’t mean every robot needs legs or even that every robot needs to look like a person.

For a lot of tasks, a mobile base with wheels and a couple of arms could be really useful. And in more specialized settings, you might want something with a completely different shape, designed around the particular task.

The thing I’m excited about is whether we can share intelligence across those different robots. If one robot learns something about manipulating an object, can that experience help another robot with a different body? If we can do that well, we don’t have to settle on a single form factor. We can have a diversity of hardware that’s appropriate for different environments, while benefiting from learning across all of it.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a wide range of robot form factors and says shared learning across robots with different bodies could support a diversity of hardware.

r002.rationale: It mentions task-specific shapes, but does not envision household robots specialized by task or compare them to kitchen appliances.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see a pretty wide range of form factors. Humanoids are compelling because we’ve built our environments for humans. If you want a robot to use the same tools, reach the same shelves, and move through the same spaces that we do, a human-like body makes sense. But that doesn’t necessarily mean two legs are the best choice for every application. In a lot of indoor environments, wheels might be simpler and more reliable.

One of the questions I’m excited about is whether we can build intelligence that transfers across those different bodies. Can a robot learn something about manipulating objects that’s useful whether it has one arm, two arms, or a different kind of gripper? If we can do that, then we have a lot more freedom to choose the hardware for the task. I’d expect both general-purpose robots and more specialized robots, rather than one form factor that wins everywhere.

r001.rationale: It expects a wide range of robot bodies and says intelligence that transfers across bodies would give more freedom to choose hardware for each task.

r002.rationale: It mentions specialized robots, but does not describe hardware tailored to particular household tasks or compare it to kitchen appliances.
